candidates.title: AgentCap: Capability-Based Runtime Authorization for Secure LLM Agent Execution
candidates.summary: Language-model agents commonly collapse two decisions that security systems separate: selecting an action and determining whether that action is authorized. When a model exercises standing authority, indirect prompt injection can convert influence over its reasoning into unauthorized effects. We present AgentCap, a runtime authorization layer that externalizes this decision from the model and mediates every tool invocation through an MCP wrapper. candidates.title: TRACER: Trace-Regularized Training Against Indirect Prompt Injection
candidates.summary: Indirect prompt injection uses untrusted retrieved content, tool outputs, or agent messages to override an LLM's intended behavior. candidates.summary: Chat remains the default surface for many large language model (LLM) tasks, even as agentic tools such as OpenCode excel at coding and automation. candidates.title: WAAA! Web Adversaries Against Web Agents
candidates.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into web browsers to create agentic browsing systems that execute actions on behalf of the user. candidates.title: When AI Agents Go Off Script: How Websites Become Targets
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: An AI agent goes off script when it does something its owner did not intend. That happens in three ways. Someone else writes the script, by planting instructions in a page, email or tool the agent reads. An attacker runs the agent, and points its speed at your website. Or the agent misreads its own task and acts on the mistake. Websites sit in the middle of all three. They are where attacking agents probe for accounts and records, and they are where hidden instructions wait for the agents that browse them. The evidence is no longer theoretical. duplicates.title: AttriGuard: Defeating Indirect Prompt Injection in LLM Agents via Causal Attribution of Tool Invocations
duplicates.summary: LLM agents are highly vulnerable to Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI), where adversaries embed malicious directives in untrusted tool outputs to hijack execution. Most existing defenses treat IPI as an input-level semantic discrimination problem, which often fails to generalize to unseen payloads.
